name: Wendy Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. Can you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the crew that repairs the ridge feeder and the farm spurs below it. I have a two-year technical diploma and know the awkward poles well enough to stop a truck before it takes the wrong track. A customer’s porch light coming back on still makes a wet day worthwhile.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The climb is slower at fifty eight, and I come home to sort the rent and my partner Alan’s medicine costs. My pay is low for a crew lead, and there are few other line jobs nearby. I do not use AI; a good phone call and a checked drawing suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that a little office shortcut is fine if someone checks the work. My crew still has to climb the ridge road when the feeder trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI and would not start for a small saving. What bothers me is that our household has less than a month put aside, and my lower pay leaves little after rent and my partner Alan’s medicines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the ridge repair crew and put the small amount left after bills toward overdue van tyres. I would wait on the holiday we had talked about until the tyres and medicines are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, as usual, about money. The AI part is mild, but I am already doing sums at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are the tyres first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van gets Alan to his appointments and takes me to the early shift. Replacing worn van tyres comes before our holiday when lineworker pay barely covers medicines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you lead the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would still make the apprentice read the pole tag and check the isolation points with me before anyone climbs.

say: I would accept a small **office shortcut** if a person checks it.
I would remind the depot that **ridge repairs** still need trained climbers in weather.
think: Our **tiny reserve** and Alan’s medicine bills already make the household fragile.
My **lower pay** leaves little room to replace the van tyres and take a holiday.
do: Keep leading **ridge repairs** and check pole isolation with the apprentice.
Delay the **holiday** until van tyres and Alan’s medicines are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about existing household costs, even though AI changes little.
S0.quote: Replacing worn van tyres comes before our holiday when lineworker pay barely covers medicines.
fieldNote: Her baseline **cash pressure** explains the anxious mood in a mild AI world.
She defers a holiday for **transport and medicine**, while keeping her established repair practice.

steps.text: Keep leading ridge repairs and checking pole isolation with the apprentice
Delay the household holiday until van tyres and medicines are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office may buy faster plans, but nobody should send a crew to a line from an untested screen. I would ask who signed the work order and who checked it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners could shrink and the depot might give us less overtime or larger routes. I am one of the best on the tools, but there are few other line jobs nearby and our savings will not cover a long shortfall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the next two duty rosters and record any lost overtime against our bills. If the extra shifts disappear, Alan and I would stop the paid television package first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can handle harder repairs, but I cannot make a missing shift appear by working better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks a work order now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the isolation note before the truck rolls, and the dispatcher confirms the address. If the new system skips either person, I would put the concern in writing to my manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cut television before food?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Food is already plain in our house. The television package is one bill we can cancel without putting Alan’s health or my work travel at risk.

say: I would demand a **named checker** for AI work orders before my crew leaves the depot.
I would tell colleagues that **field repairs** still need skilled people on the line.
think: The depot could remove **overtime** or stretch routes after shrinking its planning office.
Few **nearby jobs** and almost no reserve make a pay cut hard to absorb.
do: Record **lost overtime** from the next two duty rosters against household bills.
Cancel the **television package** if extra shifts disappear.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible cut to household pay, even while her field skill remains valuable.
S1.quote: I cannot make a missing shift appear by working better.
fieldNote: Her safety objection is grounded in a specific **work-order check** she already performs.
She gives a conditional **spending cut** tied to lost overtime, not a speculative retraining promise.

steps.text: Cancel the television package if depot overtime shifts disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a 2028 thinking machine cannot climb the ridge, yet the office might cut our callouts before 2031 robots can work. I would not let a robot near a live feeder without a proper field test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The field lag helps me for a few years, but I expect the depot to cut most overtime almost at once. At sixty three when capable robots arrive, I might need the wage more than ever because Alan’s treatment costs do not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my crew on repairs and ask the depot in writing how many field shifts it expects to keep through 2031. If two rosters show a real hours cut, I would ask my grown daughter Ruth whether we could share transport costs, not move into her house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would still turn up for work, but I would lie awake counting how many weeks the savings could cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Ruth for exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, my daughter, drives past our road on her way to work. I would ask whether we can share fuel for Alan’s appointments if my shifts fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the job now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. There is no offer waiting nearby. Leaving my ridge lineworker job now would end the pay my household still has. I would stay as long as the field shifts exist.

say: The **2028 system** cannot climb, but I would demand real trials before 2031 robots touch live feeders.
I would ask the depot to state its **field staffing** plan through the robot delay.
think: I expect to lose most **overtime immediately** even though hands-on repairs may last until 2031.
Alan’s **treatment costs** and our tiny reserve could make that loss severe.
do: Keep **repair shifts** while the depot offers them.
Ask my **daughter Ruth** to share transport costs if two rosters show fewer hours.
feel: **Alarmed** enough to lose sleep over a likely hours cut and almost no savings.
S2.quote: Leaving my ridge lineworker job now would end the pay my household still has.
fieldNote: She does not assume an early exit; continuing work is a **cash necessity**.
The proposed family help is **shared fuel**, conditional on two reduced rosters.

steps.text: Keep leading ridge repairs while depot field shifts exist
Ask daughter Ruth to share transport costs after two reduced rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough for proper testing, provided the people who climb the line can refuse unsafe work. A sales film does not show a robot finding a damaged pin in sleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 might change our call sheets, but robots come in 2034. I would be older then and still need wages unless we have saved more; my job could shrink before I can afford to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the crew next year and put a fixed extra amount from each wage into an emergency account if Alan’s medicine bills allow it. I would also ask the manager for a written field trial schedule so I can see when our work might change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years gives me room to save, but it does not fill the emergency account today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What amount could you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe twenty from each pay packet, after the prescriptions are paid. If the medicine bill rises, I will not pretend we can make the transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the new robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first need to see a safe machine working on our own ridge. I am not signing up for training on a promise.

say: I would insist **climbing crews** can refuse unsafe robot trials on live lines.
I would ask for a **written schedule** showing when the depot plans field tests.
think: I may still need **wages in 2034** even if robots reduce my repair hours.
Five years gives time to build savings, but Alan’s **medicine costs** may absorb the spare cash.
do: Keep leading **ridge repairs** during the first year.
Save an extra **twenty per pay packet** only after Alan’s medicines are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about future hours, with cautious room to save if current bills allow.
S3.quote: Five years gives me room to save, but it does not fill the emergency account today.
fieldNote: Her conditional extra transfer is actual **new saving** from wages, if prescription bills permit.
She asks for information about trials while refusing to claim any **robot-control training** yet.

steps.text: Keep leading ridge repairs during the first year
Save twenty extra from each wage only after Alan’s medicines are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentice there is time to learn the old faults properly before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would still expect a person to sign for a live-line repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty eight at the thinking date. I hope to stop climbing before then, but with less than one month saved and lower pay I cannot promise that; Alan and I still have to live on something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the ridge crew going this year and sit with Alan over the household bills every three months. I would set no retirement date until we know what we can actually pay for without my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the future of the craft, anxious about our money today. Ten years is a gift of time only if we use it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this card make you retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We cannot afford an earlier exit on the present accounts. I would rather be tired from a shift than anxious about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the apprentice take from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Check the pole number with your eyes, and ask when a drawing and the site disagree. No apprentice should be ashamed to stop a job for a second look.

say: I would tell apprentices to learn **fault finding** before thinking AI and later robots alter repairs.
I would insist a **named lineworker** signs off live-line work even in 2039.
think: I hope to stop climbing before **2036**, but current savings do not make that secure.
Alan and I still depend on my **lower wage** for rent and medicine.
do: Keep the **ridge crew** working and show the apprentice how to check pole numbers.
Review **household bills** with Alan every three months before setting a retirement date.
feel: **Anxious** about today’s money, alongside unease about the future trade.
S4.quote: I would rather be tired from a shift than anxious about the rent.
fieldNote: A decade does not erase the **existing cash shortage** in this household.
She explicitly rules out **early retirement** and uses reviews to decide when any exit is affordable.

steps.text: Keep leading ridge repairs and teaching the apprentice pole checks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the depot could take away overtime before robots reach the poles, and our reserve would barely cover a month. Written staffing plans and a named safety checker would help me judge what work will remain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company will protect apprentices when a screen writes a bad work order. A new worker may be afraid to question a bad work order.

headlineQuote: A new worker may be afraid to question a bad work order.
portrait: **Wendy**, 58, is a highly skilled ridge-line crew lead with a technical diploma and long field experience.
Her **low pay**, rent, medicine bills and less than one month saved make even the plateau financially tense.
She avoids **AI tools** and insists on human safety checks before crews act on machine plans.
The **2028 case** threatens overtime before robots reach hands-on repairs, when she may still need every wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove overtime before capable robots reach ridge repairs.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan** and named safety checker would help her judge the remaining work.
